explanations: luna: The disbelievers' hearing is sealed and a covering is over their sight; this repeats the section's contrast between eyes given and eyes unable or unwilling to perceive.
terra: The rhetorical question asks whether they do not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose, directly correcting imagined secrecy.
terra: Good sent ahead is found with Allah and He sees what people do; even quiet expenditure is preserved before the observer.
luna: The ayah condemns concealing clear proofs and guidance after they were made clear; it fits the section's reading of sign-deniers as people who cover what ought to be seen.

luna: The righteous spend wealth on relatives, orphans, needy people, and those in bondage; this joins the section's orphan/poor feeding and neck release within one account of righteousness. | terra: True righteousness includes giving loved wealth to orphans and the needy and spending فِى ٱلرِّقَابِ; feeding need and freeing necks meet in the same ethical program as the pass.
luna: Asked what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, and needy people; this matches the section's close orphan and destitute recipients as concrete recipients of giving.
terra: Charity done رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ seeks human eyes and is nullified; it reverses the deed done under God's sight without dependence on being seen by people.
terra: Concealed charity to the poor is better, and Allah is fully aware of the act; invisibility to people preserves rather than erases the deed.

luna: The needy who refrain from asking are recognized by their mark, بِسِيمَاهُمْ; this meets the section's image of a person as a visible sign and its mention of the destitute covered in dust. | terra: Hiddenly needy people are recognized by their سِيمَا rather than importunate asking; a visible mark guides the observer toward the feeding obligation.

luna: What people disclose or conceal within themselves is still brought to account by Allah; it makes inner hiddenness answerable, as in the section's image. | terra: Whether people reveal what is within themselves or hide it, Allah calls them to account for it; hidden inward material becomes an explicit reckoning.

luna: Nothing in earth or heaven is hidden from Allah; this supplies a concise boundary to the man's belief that no one saw him. | terra: Nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah, a direct universal denial of the imagined unseen deed.
terra: Allah forms people in wombs however He wills, bringing the human image itself under the knowledge of the One from whom nothing is hidden in 3:5.

luna: Whether people disclose what is within themselves or conceal it, Allah knows it; this is another direct boundary on the privacy imagined in the section. | terra: The addressee is warned that Allah knows whatever is concealed within breasts or disclosed, extending observation behind outward appearance.
terra: A group conceals within themselves what they do not show the Prophet, and Allah states that He knows what they hide.
luna: The People of the Book were charged to make scripture clear and not conceal it, but cast it away; this parallels the section's contrast between visible signs and their denial or covering.

luna: The ayah says Allah is “رَقِيبًا” over people in its command to heed Him and kinship; that is the source-section root ر ق ب in its guardian/watchful sense. | terra: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا names Allah as رَقِيب over people, the divine watcher latent in the section's ر ق ب word family.
terra: فَإِنْ ءَانَسْتُم مِّنْهُمْ رُشْدًا uses the section's ء ن س family for perceiving maturity, extending sensory noticing into responsible discernment.
terra: Those who spend to be seen by people orient the act toward created observers, the opposite error to thinking no divine observer sees it.

luna: The ayah makes freeing a believing slave part of expiation; this parallels the section's فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ and uses the neck/manumission image in a legal setting. | terra: The expiation for accidental killing includes تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُّؤْمِنَةٍ, a direct Quranic occurrence of freeing a neck.
luna: During the prayer in danger, groups take turns praying while carrying weapons and remaining alert; this gives the section's guardian sense a concrete human scene of watchfulness.

luna: People may hide their speech and plans from other people, but the ayah says they cannot hide them from Allah, who is present with them in the night counsel; it directly overturns presumed privacy. | terra: They hide from people but cannot hide from Allah, who is with them while they scheme at night; this directly exposes the empty space imagined by “no one saw.”
terra: They suppose no trial will come, become blind and deaf, and after reprieve many do so again, while Allah sees what they do.

luna: One expiation option is freeing a slave, alongside feeding needy people; it closely joins the section's release of a neck with its feeding of the hungry. | terra: The expiation for a broken oath includes تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, repeating the section's concrete act in another legal setting.

luna: The ayah stages game within reach of hands and spears, then says the test is who fears Allah unseen; it joins the section's hidden hunter/prey sense to the question of conduct when people cannot see. | terra: Reachable game tests who fears Allah unseen; the hunter believes the quarry exposed, while his own hidden restraint is what Allah tests and knows.

luna: Jesus says Allah was “الرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ,” watchful over his people; the source-section root ر ق ب names this very guarding stance. | terra: Jesus contrasts his finite witnessing while among his people with Allah as ٱلرَّقِيبَ over them after his departure, clarifying the difference between human and divine surveillance.

luna: The ayah asks who could restore hearing and sight if Allah took them away; it marks the eyes as a revocable gift rather than a power a person owns. | terra: The question asks who besides Allah could restore hearing and sight if He took them, reinforcing that the organs invoked by 90:8 remain wholly His gift.

luna: The ayah asks whether the blind and the seeing are equal; this is another direct Qur'anic formulation of the perception boundary developed in the section. | terra: The Prophet denies possessing the unseen and asks whether the blind and seeing are equal, distinguishing revelation-dependent knowledge from ordinary sight.

luna: Allah knows every leaf that falls and every grain, wet or dry, recorded in a clear book; this gives the section's unseen-observer claim a concrete image of nothing escaping notice. | terra: The keys of the unseen, every fallen leaf, and every grain in darkness are known and recorded, extending the watching image to what no created eye detects.
terra: Allah sends guardians over people until death and His messengers take the soul without neglect, extending observation into custody.

luna: The ayah sets a boundary on sight: eyes do not comprehend Allah, while He comprehends all eyes; the section's eye-gift therefore does not make human vision unlimited. | terra: Eyes do not encompass Allah while He encompasses all vision; the gaze is radically asymmetric, so failure to see the watcher gives no ground for thinking oneself unseen.

luna: Clear proofs have come, and whoever sees benefits himself while whoever is blind harms himself; the verse joins visible signs, moral blindness, and the limit of a guardian, all developed in the section. | terra: بَصَآئِرُ have come from the Lord: whoever sees benefits himself and whoever is blind harms himself; the Prophet also denies being their keeper, distinguishing guidance from forced surveillance.

luna: People on the heights recognize others by their marks; the visible mark identifies a person, a concrete parallel to the section's lexicon calling a person's recognizable form an “āya.” | terra: Men on the Heights recognize every group by their marks; elevated lookout, visible signs, and identification of persons converge in a single scene.
terra: When the watchers' eyes are turned toward the Fire's people, they beg not to be placed with wrongdoers; the lofty gaze reaches the threatened fire.
terra: The people of the Heights call men they recognize by their marks, continuing the section's watch-post and visible-person senses.

luna: These people have eyes but do not see with them; this is the section's sharp reversal of the given two eyes as a faculty of perception. | terra: People have eyes with which they do not see and ears with which they do not hear; possession of the gift is reversed into culpable nonuse.

luna: Those who deny the signs are gradually drawn on from where they do not know; this parallels the section's secondary d-r-y image of a hunter approaching prey unseen, though the verse itself describes divine enticement rather than hunting.
luna: The next ayah says the deniers are given respite and that God's plan is firm; it completes the gradual, unperceived approach in 7:182.

luna: The section's dictionary describes a lookout and a hunter's hiding place; this ayah orders the pursuers to lie in wait at every ambush, a concrete scene of concealed watching in a different setting. | terra: “Sit in wait for them at every مَرْصَدٍ” supplies a human ambush or observation station, a hostile counterpart to the lookout developed from the section's roots.

luna: A share of alms is assigned “فِي الرِّقَابِ,” for freeing people from bondage; this directly parallels the section's release of a neck. | terra: Obligatory alms have a share وَفِى ٱلرِّقَابِ, institutionalizing release from bondage alongside aid to the poor and needy.
terra: The question asks whether they know that Allah knows their secret and private counsel, another pointed exposure of speech thought to lack a listener.
terra: Some hypocrites are unknown to the Prophet but known to Allah, drawing a boundary between human recognition and the observer who misses no concealed person.

luna: People are told to act because Allah, His Messenger, and the believers will see their deeds; this makes the section's unseen action explicitly visible and answerable. | terra: “Work,” then Allah, His messenger, and the believers will see the work; the command makes action explicitly answerable to multiple witnesses.
terra: The harmful mosque is built as an إِرْصَادًا, an outpost for an enemy of Allah and His messenger, giving the lookout image a covert human use.
terra: The addressee must admit that Allah controls hearing and sight, moving from possession of eyes to dependence on their provider.
luna: Some look toward the Prophet, but he cannot guide the blind who do not see; the verse distinguishes looking from true perception as the section does.

luna: The ayah says no action or state is absent from Allah, down to an atom's weight, and that it is recorded; this extends the section's unseen-observer claim to every deed and its record. | terra: No affair, recitation, or deed is entered without Allah being witness as it begins, and not even an atom escapes Him.
terra: Pharaoh's body is preserved so that he may be an ءَايَةً for those after him; a man's visible body literally becomes a sign.

luna: People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide from God, yet He knows what they conceal and reveal; this directly stages the hiddenness the section's man presumes. | terra: People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide, yet Allah knows both what they conceal and disclose; bodily concealment cannot produce an unwatched place.
terra: The two parties are likened to blind and deaf versus seeing and hearing, making responsible perception a moral distinction rather than mere possession of organs.

luna: Noah is told to make the ship under Allah's eyes and revelation; this is the section's protective-eye sense applied to a watched act. | terra: Noah is commanded to build the ark بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا; protective observation and divinely supplied knowledge accompany an act humans could not secure alone.
terra: Shuayb says وَٱرْتَقِبُوٓا۟ إِنِّى مَعَكُمْ رَقِيبٌ, using the ر ق ب family for mutual waiting and watching as judgment approaches.
terra: When the husband sees the shirt torn from behind, the material trace exposes what occurred without an eyewitness, a concrete sign disclosing a concealed act.
terra: Jacob commands his sons to seek news of Joseph and his brother, a family search for hidden persons that resembles the section's news-gathering eye.

luna: The ayah equates one who hides a statement with one who declares it, and the person hidden by night with the one abroad by day; it directly dissolves the public/private boundary in the section. | terra: Secret and public speech, hiding by night, and moving by day are equal before Allah, systematically closing every route by which the man might imagine himself unseen.

luna: Linked to 13:10, successive guardians preserve each person by Allah's command; it supplies the watcher behind the ayah's contrast of hidden and public conduct. | terra: Successive agents before and behind a person guard him by Allah's command, a mobile version of the protective watcher.
luna: The ayah asks whether the blind and the seeing, or darkness and light, are equal; it uses sight as a measure of recognition, directly matching the section's eye-and-guidance link.
terra: The Prophet is told not to suppose Allah unaware of what wrongdoers do; the repeated verb of supposition is corrected by delayed but exact observation.
luna: Wrongdoers are seen bound together in chains on the day of Judgment; this reverses the release of a neck in the section and makes the bound state visible.
terra: Allah places constellations in heaven and beautifies them for observers, providing the visible high scene that 15:17 immediately guards.
terra: The heaven is guarded from every expelled devil, supplying a cosmic instance of the section's guarding watcher.
terra: Whoever steals a hearing is followed by a clear flame, again making the covert collector of news into visible prey.
terra: The ruined settlement contains signs for those who read marks and lies on an enduring road, bringing visible signs and a travelled way together.
terra: The ruined place lies on an enduring road; this ayah, rather than 15:75 alone, supplies the roadway on which its signs remain visible.
terra: Allah knows what people conceal and what they reveal, closing the divide on which an unwatched deed depends.

luna: The example contrasts an owned slave unable to act with a person given good provision who spends openly and secretly; it joins the section's freed neck, hidden conduct, and boast about wealth in one comparison.

luna: People emerge knowing nothing, then Allah gives them hearing, sight, and hearts; the verse presents sight as a created gift that makes the section's question about its giver pointed. | terra: People leave their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts, joining divine provision of perception to acquired knowledge.

luna: Each person's deed is fastened to his neck, then brought out as an open record; this joins the section's neck and watcher details in one bodily image of unavoidable accounting. | terra: Each person's record is fastened to his neck and brought out as an open book, joining bodily neck imagery to an inescapable account.

luna: The person is told to read his book and finds himself sufficient as his own accountant; it completes 17:13 by showing what the neck-borne record requires. | terra: The person is told to read his own book and is sufficient as his own accountant; observation finally returns as self-reading.

luna: The section recalls that eyes were given to a person; this ayah says hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned, making the gifts answerable for their use. | terra: Hearing, sight, and heart are each subject to questioning, making the bestowed eye accountable rather than merely possessed.
terra: The she-camel is given as a visible sign, yet her people wrong her; a plainly shown ءَايَة can still be rejected.
terra: أَبْصِرْ بِهِۦ وَأَسْمِعْ praises Allah's perfect seeing and hearing and denies creatures any protecting partner, joining perception and guardianship.

luna: The opened book omits neither small nor great deeds, and people see what they did present before them; this gives the section's claim of unwitnessed acts an exhaustive record scene. | terra: The book omits neither small nor great and people find their deeds present; exhaustive recording makes the once-hidden act visible at judgment.
terra: The guilty see the Fire, know they are falling into it, and find no escape, another final sight of what earlier remained beyond their view.

luna: The ayah describes eyes covered from Allah's reminder and inability to hear it; it shows how an eye can be present yet barred from the signs it should perceive. | terra: Their eyes were under a covering from Allah's reminder and they could not hear, combining veiled sight with refusal of the signs.
terra: “How well they will hear and see” on the day they come to Allah contrasts their present manifest error with unavoidable later perception.
terra: هَلْ تُحِسُّ مِنْهُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَوْ تَسْمَعُ asks whether even one of the destroyed peoples can be sensed or heard, closely matching the idiom in which no eye means no person.
terra: Even if speech is voiced aloud, Allah knows the secret and what is still more hidden, placing divine hearing beyond sensory access.

luna: Moses reports “إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا,” using the source-section root ء ن س for perceiving something by sight; the scene supplies a literal instance of that dictionary sense. | terra: Moses says إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ نَارًا after perceiving a fire; it is the exact Quranic use of the section's dictionary sense of ء ن س for seeing or sensing something distant.

luna: The section's dictionary branch for ع ي ن describes keeping someone “under my eye”; Allah tells Moses he was made to grow “عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي,” an eye of care and protection. | terra: وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِى uses “My eye” for Allah's protective oversight of Moses, exactly matching the dictionary's guarding sense of عَيْن.
terra: Moses' sister walks after him and he is returned so his mother's eye may be comforted; this supplies the human watching and protective outcome surrounding 20:39's divine eye.
terra: Allah reassures Moses and Aaron, إِنَّنِى مَعَكُمَآ أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَىٰ; hearing and seeing are protective presence before the tyrant.
terra: Aaron asks why Moses did not تَرْقُبْ قَوْلِى; the root has the secondary sense of heeding or guarding a word, plausibly extending watching from persons to entrusted speech.
terra: Whoever turns from Allah's reminder is raised blind, making lost sight the consequence of refusing guidance.
terra: The raised person asks why he is blind although he once saw, explicitly confronting the difference between possessing sight and using it rightly.
terra: Allah answers that His signs came and were forgotten, so the sign-denier is now left forgotten; rejected ءَايَٰت explain the blindness.
terra: The sky is made a guarded canopy while people turn away from its signs, bringing protective watch and neglected ءَايَٰت together.
terra: Allah knows spoken words and what people conceal, a direct counterpart to the watched utterance in 50:18.

luna: The ayah says it is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts in the breasts; this sets a boundary between the section's sensory eye and inward recognition. | terra: The ayah says eyes are not what go blind, but hearts within breasts; it sets a boundary between sensory sight and the perception needed to understand the pass.

luna: The ship is built under Allah's eyes and revelation, repeating the section's ع ي ن sense of watching over and safeguarding someone or something. | terra: The repeated command to make the ark بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا again binds the watching eye to revelation and rescue.

luna: Allah says He made hearing, sight, and hearts for people, yet few give thanks; it repeats the created-senses detail and links it to accountability for a gift. | terra: Allah originates hearing, eyes, and hearts for people, another direct reminder that the faculty by which they judge visibility is itself given.

luna: On the Day of Judgment, people's tongues, hands, and feet testify to what they did; this repeats the section's image of bodily faculties becoming witnesses against their owner. | terra: Tongues, hands, and feet testify about what their owners used to do, extending the watching function beyond the two eyes.
luna: The next ayah says Allah will pay them their true recompense; it completes 24:24 by linking bodily testimony to judgment.
terra: The command not to enter others' houses until seeking recognition or permission sets a privacy boundary on the human impulse to observe what is inside.
terra: Believing men are commanded to lower their gaze, and Allah is fully aware of what they do; the bestowed eye itself falls under moral observation.
terra: Believing women are likewise commanded to lower their gaze and guard themselves, marking an ethical boundary on human looking.

luna: Slaves seeking a contract of freedom are to be given one, and helped from God's wealth; it gives another concrete Qur'anic route from bondage toward release. | terra: Owners are commanded to grant emancipation contracts to those in bondage and give them from Allah's wealth, concretely extending the freeing-neck side of the pass.
terra: The Fire itself رَأَتْهُم مِّن مَّكَانٍۭ بَعِيدٍ and they hear its rage; the expected gaze reverses, making the distant fire the watcher of its targets.
terra: Believers do not fall upon their Lord's signs deaf and blind; their reception reverses the unused eyes and denied signs in this section.
terra: The Lord يَرَىٰكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ, presenting divine sight of the Prophet's otherwise private rising.
terra: وَتَقَلُّبَكَ فِى ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ continues 26:218's gaze into the Prophet's movements among those prostrating.
terra: The close إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ completes the protective seeing scene with hearing and knowledge.

luna: Moses again says “آنَسْتُ نَارًا”; this repeats the section's dictionary use of the root ء ن س for seeing or perceiving, here in a fire-seen scene. | terra: Moses again says إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ نَارًا and expects news or a burning brand, joining perception, distant information, and fire.
terra: When visibly illuminating signs come, the people call them manifest magic; perceptibility does not prevent the sign-denier from covering what should be seen.
terra: Solomon inspects the birds and notices the hoopoe's absence, beginning a scene of a ruler's watch and a scout who gathers distant news.
terra: The absent bird must bring a clear authorization or face punishment, sharpening the accountable relation between scout and watcher.
terra: The hoopoe returns with certain news from Sheba that Solomon did not encompass, exemplifying the news-gathering “eye” and the limits of a ruler's knowledge.
terra: The Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose, making inward intention and outward act equally visible to knowledge.
terra: Pharaoh's wife calls the found infant a comfort of the eye and prevents his killing, adding human protection to the Moses-under-the-divine-eye sequence.
terra: Moses' sister sees him from a distance while his captors do not perceive her; a hidden watcher gathers news over the child already placed under Allah's eye.
terra: Moses is restored to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may know Allah's promise is true, completing 28:11's distant watch.
terra: Moses spends the morning in the city خَآئِفًا يَتَرَقَّبُ, watchfully awaiting danger; the watcher here is a vulnerable fugitive.
terra: Moses leaves the city fearful and يَتَرَقَّبُ, continuing the root's sense of alert waiting while himself exposed to pursuit.

luna: In the third telling Moses says “آنَسْتُ نَارًا”; it repeats the source-section root's sense of seeing something, with the fire as the noticed object. | terra: Moses perceives a fire from the mountain's side and hopes for news or an ember; the ء ن س sense, remote sign, lookout height, and fire all meet.
terra: The Lord knows what breasts conceal and what people disclose, repeated in a judgment context where He chooses and decides.
terra: A clear sign is left from the destroyed town for people who reason, an enduring visible trace that must be interpreted rather than merely looked at.
terra: The dwellings of ʿAd and Thamud are visibly evident, yet Satan barred them from the way although they had insight; visible remains, perception, and a blocked path converge.

luna: After forming the human and breathing life into him, Allah makes hearing, sight, and hearts; this is another direct account of the eye as something bestowed by its Maker. | terra: After shaping the human and breathing spirit into him, Allah makes hearing, eyes, and hearts; bodily form and perceptive gifts share one Creator.
terra: The guilty finally say “we have seen and heard” and ask to return, but perception arrives after the arena of responsible action has closed.

luna: The ayah closes with Allah as رَقِيبًا over all things, repeating the source-section root ر ق ب in its watchful-guardian sense. | terra: وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ رَّقِيبًا gives the section's watcher-root its unrestricted divine scope.
luna: The question “وَمَا يُدْرِيكَ” asks what could make the Prophet know, then says the Hour may be near; this echoes the section's root for what is disclosed about an unknown reality.
terra: Not an atom in heavens or earth is absent from Allah, and nothing smaller or greater escapes a clear record; this joins minute observation to writing.
luna: The ayah says shackles will be put around the disbelievers' necks; it turns the section's freed neck into a sign of judgment's restraint.
luna: The blind and the seeing are declared unequal; this repeats the section's physical and moral sight contrast in a brief direct formulation.
luna: The ayah describes shackles placed on the disbelievers' necks; this reverses the section's freeing of a neck, and its next ayah adds that their sight is blocked.
luna: A barrier before and behind them leaves them unable to see; linked to 36:8, it joins bound necks to blocked vision, meeting two elements of the section's image.
terra: Allah writes what people send ahead and the traces they leave, having enumerated everything in a clear register.

luna: The mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people earned; it repeats the bodily testimony scene with a different set of organs. | terra: Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned; the body supplies the witness the person imagined absent.

luna: Allah says He could wipe out their eyes, after which they would rush toward the path but not see; this reverses the eye as a dependable gift and joins sight to guidance. | terra: Allah could obliterate their eyes as they race for the path, leaving them unable to see; eye and road are joined by the withdrawal of the gift.
terra: The adorned heaven is protected from every rebellious devil, supplying the guarding action that 37:8-10 continues with attempted eavesdropping.
terra: The rebellious devils cannot listen to the highest assembly and are pelted from every side, making illicit news-gathering the object of vigilant defense.
terra: They are driven away and assigned lasting punishment, the consequence of breaching the guarded listening scene.
terra: The one who snatches a fragment of hearing is pursued by a piercing flame, a concise spy-and-hunter reversal.

luna: The source image joins a watching eye to what is hidden; this ayah names both “خَائِنَةَ الْأَعْيُنِ” and what breasts conceal, including a furtive glance and inward secrecy. | terra: Allah knows خَآئِنَةَ ٱلْأَعْيُنِ and what breasts hide, making even the eye's covert betrayal visible to the watcher.
terra: The believing speaker entrusts his affair to Allah because Allah sees the servants, making divine sight the ground of protection amid a hostile plot.
luna: The blind and seeing are not equal, nor are believers who do good and the evildoer; this explicitly joins perception with the moral distinction made in the section.
terra: Allah formed people and made their forms good, plausibly extending the section's small human image to the divine fashioning of every bodily form.
luna: The people of Hell are described with shackles and chains around their necks; this is a direct bodily reversal of the section's emancipation image.
luna: They are dragged into boiling water and then the Fire; linked to 40:71, it completes the scene of those bound by the neck.
terra: Only when people see Allah's might do they profess belief and reject their former partners; perception arrives after their prior signs were denied.
terra: Belief no longer benefits once divine might is seen, establishing the temporal boundary between responsible trust and compelled sight.

luna: Thamud were shown guidance but preferred blindness to it; the ayah makes sight's moral refusal explicit, beyond the physical eye described in the section. | terra: Thamud are guided but prefer blindness to guidance, making chosen moral blindness the contrary of using the bestowed eye to take the shown road.

luna: The section treats the two eyes as a gift and a witness; here ears, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, turning the organs into evidence. | terra: At the Fire, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners; the given eye becomes a witness against the person who assumed he was unseen.
terra: The skins explain that Allah, who makes everything speak, made them speak; the Creator of bodily perception can turn the body into testimony.

luna: The section's imagined privacy is stated almost exactly in the condemned people's thought that Allah did not know much of what they did; the verse names the false premise behind acting unseen. | terra: وَلَٰكِن ظَنَنتُمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَعْلَمُ names the very delusion behind 90:7: they supposed Allah did not know much of what they did.
terra: This ayah says that their supposition about their Lord ruined them, completing the consequence of the unseen-observer delusion named in 41:22.
terra: ٱعْمَلُوا۟ مَا شِئْتُمْ is immediately bounded by إِنَّهُۥ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ, turning apparent freedom from observers into a warning of exact sight.

luna: Allah promises to show signs in the horizons and within people until the truth is clear; this gives the section's dictionary link between ayat and visible signs a direct Qur'anic counterpart. | terra: Allah will show signs in the horizons and in themselves until truth becomes clear, then asks whether the Lord's witnessing of everything suffices.

luna: After naming the revealed Book and balance, the ayah asks what could make the hearer know that the Hour may be near; it repeats the source-section root د ر ي around knowledge not controlled by people.
luna: The Prophet says he had not known the Book or faith before revelation; the source-section root د ر ي likewise marks the human limit that God's disclosure can cross.

luna: The people ask whether God hears their secret counsel, and the answer says the messengers are present recording it; hidden speech in the section's image is likewise not unwitnessed. | terra: أَمْ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّا لَا نَسْمَعُ asks whether they suppose secret speech is unheard, then says the messengers beside them write it; it is the auditory counterpart of 90:7.

luna: The command to “watch for” the coming day uses ارتقب from the source-section root ر ق ب, in the section's sense of watching and awaiting what is coming. | terra: فَٱرْتَقِبْ asks the Prophet to watch for the day the sky brings visible smoke, joining expectant watching to a sign appearing overhead.
luna: The awaited smoke covers people and is a painful torment; it completes 44:10 by showing what the root ر ق ب commands the hearer to watch for.

luna: The closing command “watch; they too are watching” repeats the source-section root ر ق ب as waiting for an outcome. | terra: فَٱرْتَقِبْ إِنَّهُم مُّرْتَقِبُونَ sets the Prophet's waiting against the opponents' waiting, a reciprocal use of the section's watcher-root.
luna: After describing a person who makes desire his god, the ayah says Allah seals hearing and heart and places a covering over sight; it reverses the eyes' gift into impaired perception.

luna: The record speaks truth and states that what people did was being written; this repeats the section's image of actions made present as testimony. | terra: Allah's book speaks truth against them because their deeds were being copied, turning ongoing observation into documentary testimony.

luna: Past peoples were given hearing, sight, and hearts, but these availed them nothing when they denied the signs; the senses in the section can be received yet refused as instruments of recognition. | terra: Hearing, eyes, and hearts avail a people nothing because they reject Allah's signs; the given faculties and denied ءَايَٰت are brought together exactly.

luna: After battle, captives may be released by grace or ransom; it is a parallel act of releasing bound people, though the context is prisoners of war rather than a slave's neck. | terra: فَضَرْبَ ٱلرِّقَابِ stages striking necks in battle, then binding and eventual release or ransom; it is the violent boundary against which “freeing a neck” is heard.
terra: Those with diseased hearts suppose Allah will not expose their rancor, another false supposition that concealed inward reality can escape disclosure.

luna: The Prophet is told he would recognize the hypocrites by their marks and speech; visible appearance functions as a sign of the person, parallel to the source-section's secondary āya sense. | terra: Hypocrites could be recognized by their marks and are known through the tone of speech, while Allah knows all deeds; appearance, hearing, and divine knowledge overlap.
luna: The believers' mark is visible on their faces; this is a bodily identifier parallel to the section's secondary āya sense of a person's visible form.

luna: The command وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا forbids spying on one another; it gives the section's secondary image of an eye sent to gather news a human setting and a moral boundary. | terra: وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا۟ forbids spying, setting a moral boundary around the human “eye” that gathers news even while divine observation remains unrestricted.

luna: The section says the creator of eyes knows seeing; here the Creator says He knows the soul's whispered thoughts and is nearer than the jugular vein, extending oversight beyond what an eye can observe. | terra: Allah says He created the human, knows the soul's whisper, and is nearer than the jugular; creation, hidden thought, and intimate observation meet in one ayah.
terra: The two receivers seated at right and left stage the watchers whose recording presence 50:18 brings to the man's speech.

luna: The section connects the spoken claim in 90:6 with a watching presence; this ayah says no word is uttered without a ready recorder, using the source-section root ر ق ب in رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ. | terra: No word is uttered without a ready رَقِيبٌ beside it; this directly joins 90:6's speech to the watcher hidden in the root of رَقَبَةٍ.
luna: Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, سَائِقٌ وَشَهِيدٌ; this makes the section's unseen watcher an explicit companion at judgment.
luna: The ayah says the covering is removed and sight becomes sharp, “فَبَصَرُكَ الْيَوْمَ حَدِيدٌ”; it reverses the section's man's imagined control of what can be seen by making the hidden clear.
luna: A recognized share of wealth belongs to the petitioner and deprived; this makes the section's feeding of the hungry a matter of others' due, not merely private generosity.
terra: The earth contains ءَايَٰتٌ for the certain, presenting signs as perceptible marks distributed before the observer.
terra: وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ turns the gaze onto the observers' own bodies, as the section turns from “no one saw” to the eyes given to the speaker.

luna: The Prophet is told to be patient under Allah's eyes; this directly echoes the section's dictionary phrase for someone kept and watched over. | terra: فَإِنَّكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا places the Prophet under divine eyes while he waits patiently, another direct Quranic realization of the protective-eye idiom.
terra: The heart does not falsify what it saw, linking inward apprehension to the trustworthy vision later bounded in 53:17.
terra: مَا زَاغَ ٱلْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَىٰ presents sight that neither swerves nor exceeds its limit, a precise boundary for the seeing faculty.
terra: The seer beholds some of his Lord's greatest signs, joining disciplined vision in 53:17 to signs that truly must be seen.
luna: The ayah says a person's striving will be seen, سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ; it directly joins the section's sight motif to deeds and their recompense.

luna: Noah's ark sails under Allah's eyes; the section's protective-eye meaning is pictured as oversight of the vessel through the flood. | terra: The ark runs بِأَعْيُنِنَا as recompense for the one denied, turning divine eyes into sustained guardianship through danger.
terra: فَٱرْتَقِبْهُمْ وَٱصْطَبِرْ commands Salih to watch his people during the she-camel test, making observation part of waiting for their response to a sign.
terra: Everything people did is in written records, directly denying that any deed passed without preservation.
terra: Every small and great thing is inscribed, completing 54:52's record with the same exhaustive scale as the observing eye.

luna: Criminals are recognized by their marks and seized; the section's dictionary sense of a person's visible form as an āya is echoed by the body serving as an identifying sign. | terra: The guilty are recognized by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet, making the visible person an identified target at judgment.

luna: Allah's statement that He is with people wherever they are and sees what they do restates the section's claim that an unseen act remains in view. | terra: هُوَ مَعَكُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُمْ and His sight of deeds place every human location within the observing presence that 90:7 denies.
terra: Allah hears the woman who argues concerning her husband and her dialogue with the Prophet; a private human complaint is already heard and seen.

luna: A man who makes the forbidden comparison about his wife must free a slave before returning to her; this repeats the section's act of freeing a neck in a different legal context. | terra: The expiation for returning from ẓihār begins with تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, another direct freeing of a neck.
luna: If he cannot free a slave, he must fast, then feed sixty poor people if unable; the neighbor ayah completes 58:3 and explicitly moves from manumission to feeding.
terra: Allah has enumerated deeds that people forgot and is witness over everything, showing that human forgetting does not erase observed action.

luna: Even a private conversation among three has Allah as the fourth, and He informs them of their deeds on the Day of Resurrection; the ayah makes secrecy no shelter from the watcher. | terra: Every secret council has Allah with it, however its members count themselves, and He will tell them their deeds; supposed privacy becomes witnessed account.
terra: The expelled people thought their fortresses would protect them, but Allah reached them from where they did not expect and tells possessors of sight to take heed.
terra: Allah formed people and perfected their forms, then states that the final return is to Him; visible form and return to its maker are joined.
terra: Allah knows heaven and earth, concealed and disclosed acts, and what breasts contain, gathering all levels of hiddenness under one knowledge.
terra: The Fire has stern angelic keepers who never disobey Allah, another direct meeting of fire with vigilant guardians.
terra: Lamps adorn the nearest heaven and become missiles against devils, so distant visible lights also enforce the guarded boundary.
terra: The people of the blaze admit that listening or reasoning would have kept them from the Fire, exposing their failure to use the faculties given in 67:23.

luna: Whether people conceal or declare their speech, Allah knows what is within their breasts; it directly joins hidden words to inward knowledge. | terra: Whether speech is concealed or voiced, Allah knows what is within breasts; both the secret word and its inward source remain observed.
terra: أَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَنْ خَلَقَ asks whether the One who created could fail to know, answering the section's question whether the maker of the eye could fail to see.

luna: Allah says He brought people into being and gave them hearing, sight, and hearts; this directly answers the section's question about who made the eyes and what their gift implies. | terra: The One who originated people made hearing, eyes, and hearts for them; it directly parallels the reminder “Did We not make him two eyes?”
terra: When the promised punishment is seen near, the deniers' faces darken and they are told this is what they demanded, turning denied warning into immediate sight.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, showing hidden divine action around people plotting to withhold provision.
terra: The garden owners whisper that no needy person should enter that day, a concealed refusal of feeding that the surrounding divine visitation exposes.
luna: Those who deny the Reminder are gradually drawn on from where they do not know; this repeats the specific unseen-approach image in 7:182 and the section's hunter/prey lexical image.
luna: The next ayah grants them respite; it completes the unseen gradual drawing in 68:44.
terra: The deniers almost strike the Prophet with their eyes when they hear the reminder, making the gaze itself a hostile means of targeting a visible person.

luna: The question “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الْحَاقَّةُ” repeats the source-section's formula for something whose reality the hearer cannot supply unaided. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْحَآقَّةُ uses divine disclosure for the reality of judgment in the same surah where the left-handed person later says he did not know his account.

luna: People are brought forward with no hidden thing of theirs concealed; this states the opposite of the left-hand man's imagined privacy and leads into the book scenes. | terra: On the day of exposure, لَا تَخْفَىٰ مِنكُمْ خَافِيَةٌ states that no hidden thing belonging to a person remains hidden.
luna: The person given his book in his right hand says to read it; this supplies the opposite book-receiving outcome to 69:25–26, which the section cites.
luna: He says he knew he would meet his account; it completes 69:19 and contrasts with the left-hand speaker's not knowing his account in 69:26.
luna: This ayah identifies the speaker in 69:26 as the one given his book in his left hand; it is the needed context for the section's quotation of his words.

luna: The person given his book in his left hand says he did not know what his account was; this is the section's exact د ر ي example of knowledge turned back on the speaker. | terra: The left-handed speaker says وَلَمْ أَدْرِ مَا حِسَابِيَهْ, turning the section's د ر ي verb inward when the once-unseen account is handed to him.
luna: The condemned man is seized and shackled; this is the reversal of the section's “فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ,” a freed neck turned into punishment by restraint.
luna: He is then cast into the Blaze; linked to 69:30 and 69:32, this completes the restrained man's punishment in the same left-hand-book scene that the section invokes at 69:26.
luna: A chain of seventy cubits is placed around him; linked to 69:30, it intensifies the opposite of the section's freed neck.
luna: The condemned person did not believe in Allah; linked to 69:34, this pairs disbelief with the failure to feed the poor, against the section's joined faith and mercy.

luna: The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; this is the direct negative counterpart to the section's hungry-day feeding. | terra: The left-handed person's account includes his failure to urge feeding the needy, connecting his “I did not know my account” in 69:26 to the food side of surah 90's answer.
terra: The jinn find heaven filled with powerful guards and flames, staging a defended observation post against would-be gatherers of hidden news.

luna: The jinn describe sitting at stations to gather news by listening; this parallels the source-section's dictionary sense of عَيْن as a scout sent to collect news, though the Qur'anic scouts listen rather than look. | terra: Those who sat in listening stations now find a flame lying in wait, combining spying for news, a lookout seat, and fiery ambush.

luna: Allah does not disclose His unseen to أَحَدًا, “anyone”; this meets the section's link between أَحَدٌ (“anyone”) and عين (“eye”) in a verse about who may know what is hidden. | terra: The Knower of the unseen discloses His unseen to no one except a chosen messenger, sharply marking what a human cannot know until God informs him.

luna: The next ayah makes an exception for a chosen messenger and places guards before and behind him; it completes 72:26 with both disclosure and watchfulness. | terra: Allah sends guards before and behind the chosen messenger, joining communicated knowledge to an encircling watch.

luna: The ayah says Allah encompasses what the messengers have and counts everything; it completes 72:26–27 by confirming the disclosure and the full accounting around it. | terra: The guarded disclosure establishes that the messages were delivered and that Allah encompasses and counts all things.
luna: The ayah names chains and a blazing fire prepared for the guilty; this is a contrary fate to the section's freeing of a neck.
luna: It adds food that chokes and painful punishment; linked to 73:12, it extends the punishment scene opposite the section's feeding of the hungry.
terra: The solitary man of the passage is given extensive wealth, linking the later fire question to a figure who treats provision as grounds for resistance.
terra: He stubbornly opposes Allah's signs, identifying the fire-bound figure as the same kind of sign-denier named at the end of surah 90.
terra: سَأُرْهِقُهُۥ صَعُودًا promises him a punishing ascent, a dark counterpart to the difficult pass whose ascent consists in freeing and feeding.

luna: The speaker says he will cast the man into Saqar; it frames the “what is Saqar?” question in 74:27 that the section cites as a fire-opening formula. | terra: سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ places the wealthy sign-denier into Saqar immediately before another “what will make you know?” question.

luna: This is another “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ” question, this time about Saqar; the section specifically says the formula often opens onto fire. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا سَقَرُ is a third direct case where the section's formula opens onto fire.
luna: Saqar neither leaves nor spares; linked to 74:27, this supplies the fire's consequence after the question.

luna: The next ayah says Saqar scorches people; it completes the fire description following 74:27 and 74:28. | terra: لَوَّاحَةٌ لِّلْبَشَرِ describes Saqar as scorching or visibly altering human skin, fitting the bodily witness and watched human of this image.
terra: عَلَيْهَا تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ places nineteen over the Fire, adding appointed overseers to the fire disclosed by 74:27.
terra: The keepers of the Fire are angels and their number is a trial that exposes belief and doubt; divine knowledge fixes what human speculation cannot.
luna: Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned; this is a boundary opposite to the section's freeing of a neck.
luna: The next ayah excepts the people of the right; it completes 74:38 with the divided outcome echoed by the section's companions of the right and left.
luna: The condemned are asked what brought them into Saqar; it introduces the punishment whose answer in 74:44 includes failure to feed the poor.

luna: People in Saqar say they were not among those who fed the poor; this directly contrasts the section's feeding of the hungry with a deed associated with punishment. | terra: The people of Saqar confess that they did not feed the needy, directly joining the fire disclosed in 74:27 to neglect of the act disclosed in 90:14-16.
terra: The human will be told what he sent ahead and left behind, making unseen consequences part of the disclosed account.

luna: The section's “insān of the eye” is a small image of the person seen within another's pupil; here a person is described as a witness against himself, turning the self into its own evidence. | terra: بَلِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٌ makes the human a witness against himself, even before the bodily testimony developed elsewhere.
luna: The self remains witness even if it offers excuses; it completes 75:14 by showing that self-testimony cannot be evaded.

luna: The human is created and tested, then made hearing and seeing; this connects the section's created eyes to the moral testing of what a person does while seen. | terra: The human is created from a mixed drop for testing and made hearing and seeing, so perception is both gift and part of accountability.
luna: The disbelievers are prepared chains, shackles, and fire; this is the bodily opposite of the section's release of a neck and its contrast between the two final groups.

luna: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive; this brings together the section's feeding of the hungry and its release of a neck, with mercy extended even to a captive. | terra: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, closely matching the concrete acts by which 90:12 explains the pass.
terra: They feed solely for Allah's face, seeking neither reward nor thanks; the act's unseen intention is known to the divine watcher.

luna: “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الْفَصْلِ” uses the same source-section question formula about the Day of Decision, a reality the question makes the hearer await. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلْفَصْلِ uses the same God-given-knowledge formula for the decisive day when hidden responsibility is separated out.
luna: The next ayah warns of woe to deniers on that day; it completes the question at 77:14 with its consequence for those who reject it.
terra: إِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ كَانَتْ مِرْصَادًا makes Hell an ambush or watch post, joining the lookout image directly to the fire disclosed by the section's questions.
terra: Everything has been counted in a book, so the eventual account rests on a complete record rather than recalled appearances.
luna: The opening rebuke concerns turning away when the blind man came; linked to 80:2, it makes the section's physical eye and the limits of sight relevant to who seeks guidance.
luna: The visitor is described as blind; this gives the section's contrast between the eye and blindness a human scene in which lack of sight does not remove the need to be heard.
luna: The next ayah asks what could make the Prophet know whether the man might purify himself; its د ر ي wording echoes the section's question about what human beings can know and what is disclosed.

luna: The passage describes the person who considers himself self-sufficient, وَأَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَىٰ; this is a close parallel to the section's wealthy man who imagines himself beyond anyone's power or sight.
luna: The addressee attends to the self-sufficient man; it completes 80:5 and sharpens the contrast with the blind seeker who follows.

luna: The following scene turns to a blind man who comes seeking guidance; unlike the affluent self-satisfied person, he is the one asking for attention, paralleling the section's care for the poor and its limits of sight.
luna: The blind visitor comes with concern and fear; it completes 80:8 by showing his earnest stance, which makes the turning-away in 80:10 consequential.
luna: The addressee is distracted from the blind seeker; it completes the scene begun in 80:8 and contrasts with the section's call to feed and aid those in need.
luna: The written records are spread open; this is a specific afterlife scene of deeds becoming visible, fitting the section's account of unwitnessed acts.
terra: Every soul will know what it has brought, the moment recorded action becomes self-knowledge.
terra: The messenger is seen on the clear horizon, a visible person at a distance that closely realizes the dictionary's “man's sign is his visible form.”
terra: The human is asked what deluded him concerning his generous Lord, opening the creation-to-guardians sequence with a false confidence like 90:7's.
terra: The Lord created, proportioned, and balanced the human, identifying the maker whose knowledge precedes the observing guardians in 82:10.
terra: Allah assembled the human in whatever form He willed, a direct Quranic counterpart to the section's attention to the human image.

luna: The section's root ر ق ب includes a guardian; this ayah says guardians are assigned over people, making the unseen watcher an explicit Qur'anic scene. | terra: وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَٰفِظِينَ places guardians over people, filling the supposed absence of an observer.

luna: Linked to 82:10, this ayah identifies the guardians as noble recording scribes; it explains what their watching does. | terra: كِرَامًا كَٰتِبِينَ identifies the guardians of 82:10 as honored recorders.

luna: Completing 82:10–11, this ayah says the scribes know what people do, specifying the conduct their record covers. | terra: يَعْلَمُونَ مَا تَفْعَلُونَ gives the recorders exact knowledge of deeds, the consequence denied by 90:7.

luna: This ayah asks “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ,” repeating the source-section's question-formula about what cannot be grasped without disclosure. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ asks for disclosure of the day on which the guardians' records become account.

luna: It repeats the question about the Day of Judgment; the repetition completes the doubled question started in 82:17. | terra: The question “what will make you know the Day of Judgment?” is repeated, stressing human inability to see that reality unaided.

luna: The answer says no soul can help another and command that day belongs to Allah; it completes 82:17–18 by stating the boundary of human power. | terra: No soul controls anything for another and command belongs to Allah, answering the repeated question with the boundary of human power.
terra: The wicked person's record is in Sijjin, supplying the object about which 83:8 asks and 83:9 answers “an inscribed book.”

luna: The same “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ” form asks what Sijjin is; as in the section, a question marks knowledge that must be supplied rather than presumed. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا سِجِّينٌ uses the disclosure formula for the destination of the wicked record.

luna: Sijjin is identified as a written record; it completes the question in 83:8 with an image of deeds fixed in a record, consonant with the section's unseen watcher. | terra: كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ answers with an inscribed record, linking God-given knowledge to the permanent recording of supposedly unseen acts.
terra: The righteous person's record is in Illiyyin, supplying the counterpart about which 83:19 asks and 83:20 answers.

luna: This ayah repeats the question-formula for Illiyyun, extending the section's examples beyond questions answered by fire. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا عِلِّيُّونَ repeats the formula for the righteous record's high repository.
luna: Illiyyun is identified as a written record; it completes 83:19 by making the unknown a record of deeds. | terra: كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ again makes the answer a written record.

luna: The next ayah says those brought near witness that record; it completes the image in 83:20 with observers, meeting the section's watcher theme. | terra: يَشْهَدُهُ ٱلْمُقَرَّبُونَ says those brought near witness that record, completing writing with present witnesses.
terra: إِنَّهُۥ ظَنَّ أَن لَّن يَحُورَ states the complacent man's false supposition; 84:15 answers it with the Lord who had always seen him, as 90:7 answers a false supposition about being unseen.

luna: The man thought he would never return, but the ayah says his Lord had always seen him; this reverses the section's imagined freedom from observation. | terra: After the man supposed he would never return, بَلَىٰ إِنَّ رَبَّهُۥ كَانَ بِهِۦ بَصِيرًا overturns his supposition with the Lord's continuous sight, closely matching 90:7's structure.
terra: وَشَاهِدٍ وَمَشْهُودٍ pairs watcher and watched as an oath, distilling the relation around which this section is built.
terra: The persecutors sit as witnesses to what they do to believers, a grim human watching scene itself enclosed by Allah's witness in 85:9.
terra: وَٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ شَهِيدٌ places the watchers of 85:7 under the universal divine witness.
terra: The oath by heaven and the night visitor begins a sequence whose distant piercing sign leads to the guardian over every soul.

luna: The question “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الطَّارِقُ” repeats the source-section's formula and points to a visible night-comer in the next ayah. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلطَّارِقُ asks for divinely given knowledge of the night visitor, preparing the visible answer and the guardian over every soul.

luna: The answer is “النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ,” a piercing star; it completes 86:2 with a visible sign in the night sky. | terra: ٱلنَّجْمُ ٱلثَّاقِبُ answers with the piercing star, a remote visible marker like the section's sign seen from afar.

luna: The section's watcher/guardian senses are made universal here: every soul has a protector over it, even though this ayah uses حَافِظ rather than the source-section root. | terra: إِن كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَّمَّا عَلَيْهَا حَافِظٌ states that every soul has a guardian over it, a compact answer to the imagined vacant watch post.
terra: فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مِمَّ خُلِقَ turns the guarded human of 86:4 into an observer commanded to inspect his own creation.
luna: The day when hidden matters are exposed, تَبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ, gives a direct counterpart to the section's insistence that what seems unseen will become known.

luna: After naming the destroyed peoples, this ayah says the Lord is “بِالْمِرْصَادِ,” at a watchful post; it makes the section's lookout image a statement about divine oversight. | terra: إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِٱلْمِرْصَادِ places the Lord at a watch post, directly realizing the section's mountaintop lookout and denying any unobserved deed.
luna: A person with abundant provision says his Lord has honored him; this parallels the section's wealthy man's assumption that material spending proves his security.
luna: The person interprets reduced provision as humiliation; the surah immediately corrects that judgment by pointing to neglect of the orphan and poor, reversing wealth as a measure of worth.

luna: This ayah condemns failing to honor the orphan; linked to 89:18, it begins the opposite of the section's care for the orphan and poor. | terra: The wealth passage following the Lord's watch post charges people with failing to honor the orphan, matching the orphan named in surah 90's feeding scene.

luna: The people do not urge one another to feed the poor; this reverses the section's feeding on a day of hunger and shows communal neglect. | terra: Immediately before the Lord-at-the-watch-post image of 89:14 gives way to judgment of wealth, people are charged with not urging one another to feed the needy.
terra: They consume inherited wealth greedily, continuing the watched community's misuse of provision after neglecting orphan and needy.

luna: The ayah says people love wealth intensely; this sharpens the parallel to the man who boasts of spending heaps of money while leaving the needy uncared for. | terra: They love wealth with consuming love, supplying the motive behind the failures that the following surah's pass reverses.
terra: The one who is miserly and deems himself self-sufficient closely matches the wealth-secure human whose supposition of independence the section exposes.
terra: He denies the best promise, joining withheld wealth to denial of what divine disclosure presents as true.
terra: Allah eases him toward hardship, a grim counter-direction to the humane ascent through the pass.
terra: His wealth does not avail when he falls, answering the boastful reliance on accumulated wealth.
luna: The orphan is not to be oppressed; this reverses the neglect of vulnerable people that the section contrasts with mercy.
luna: The person who asks is not to be repelled; this reverses the section's call to feed and aid the needy.

luna: Allah teaches the human what he did not know; this gives the section's point about what cannot be known without disclosure a concrete parallel. | terra: Allah taught the human what he did not know, closely matching the section's claim that the pass must be made known by God.
terra: The human transgresses, identifying the conduct whose supposedly unwatched instance culminates in 96:14's question about Allah seeing.
terra: The human transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient; his mistaken self-sight is answered by Allah's sight in 96:14.
terra: “Have you seen the one who forbids?” turns the audience's gaze toward the offender whom 96:14 places under Allah's gaze.
terra: The offender stops a servant while he prays, supplying the specific visible act judged by 96:14.

luna: The section asks whether anyone saw the man; this rebuke asks whether the one obstructing prayer knows that Allah sees him, making the denied observer explicit. | terra: The rhetorical question أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ directly answers the man's supposition that no one saw him: the obstructer is himself seen by Allah.
terra: Allah will summon the guards of Hell against the defiant offender, filling the scene around the watched man with appointed enforcers.
luna: The ayah asks “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ,” repeating the source-section's question about something the hearer cannot know unaided.
luna: The next ayah says the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months; it completes the unknown named in 97:2 with its revealed measure.

luna: Against the assumption that no one saw the person, the ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it: “يَرَهُ.” The deed returns to its doer as visible consequence. | terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good يَرَهُۥ; the doer himself ultimately sees the deed he might have thought no observer saw.

luna: The next ayah completes 99:7 by saying an atom's weight of evil will also be seen; the section's point about no deed being unwitnessed thus includes the reverse moral case. | terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil يَرَهُۥ, completing the two-sided return of every deed to sight.
terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْقَارِعَةُ begins the surah's first disclosure, before the second question narrows from the event to the blazing fate of light scales.
luna: Heavy scales bring a good life, the explicit reverse of the light scales and fire the section names.
luna: The pleasant life completes the heavy-scale side of the contrast with the light-scaled person in 101:8–11.

luna: The section explicitly recalls the one whose scales are light; this ayah supplies that condition, which leads into the question and fire in 101:10–11. | terra: The person whose scales are light supplies the judged subject of the disclosure question in 101:10.

luna: The ayah says his destination is “هَاوِيَةٌ”; linked to 101:10–11, it begins the answer to what awaits the person with light scales. | terra: His destination is a hāwiyah, the still-unknown reality that 101:10 asks about and 101:11 identifies as blazing fire.

luna: The section quotes “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا هِيَهْ” as an example of the source-section root د ر ي opening a question about the unknown; this is that exact question. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا هِيَهْ repeats 90:12's disclosure question, but here the unknown destination belongs to the person whose scales are light.

luna: The answer is “نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ”; it completes the question at 101:10 and makes explicit the fire the section says this formula often reveals. | terra: نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ answers 101:10 with scorching fire, while the same question in surah 90 answers with liberating and feeding.

luna: The section describes a person gathering and counting wealth; this ayah says he amassed wealth and counted it, the behavior that frames the question in 104:5. | terra: The target of the Crusher gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, closely resembling the wealth-boaster whose claim in surah 90 is made under an unacknowledged gaze.

luna: The wealth-counter thinks his wealth will make him last forever; this exposes the self-security behind the counting that the section connects to the question and fire. | terra: He supposes his wealth makes him immortal, another wealth-based supposition exposed by the coming fire and divine account.

luna: The ayah says the wealth-counter will be thrown into the Crusher; it introduces the question at 104:5 and its fire-answer in 104:6. | terra: The wealth-counter will be cast into the Crusher, setting the event that 104:5 asks the addressee to have disclosed.

luna: The section quotes “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الْحُطَمَةُ” as another use of its د ر ي question formula, here following the wealth-counter. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْحُطَمَةُ repeats the formula that tells the addressee what unaided sight cannot discover.

luna: The answer is the kindled fire of Allah; it completes 104:5 and exemplifies the fire-answer the section draws out from this formula. | terra: نَارُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ answers the disclosure question with Allah's kindled fire, the explicit reversal of 90:12-16's humane answer.
luna: The next ayah says the fire rises over hearts; it completes the fire scene after 104:6, showing the punishment reaches inward as well as burning visibly.
terra: إِنَّهَا عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ makes that fire closed over them, exactly echoing surah 90's own closing fire after the sign-denier's failed supposition.
luna: The surah opens by asking who denies the Judgment; linked to 107:2–3, this introduces denial joined to neglect of the orphan and poor, a reversal of the section's faith and mercy.

luna: The denier repels the orphan; linked to 107:3, it adds the orphan to the neglected poor and reverses the section's mercy toward both. | terra: The judgment-denier repels the orphan, supplying the first concrete failure before 107:3's refusal to urge feeding the needy.

luna: The denier does not urge feeding the poor; this is a direct negation of the section's act of feeding the hungry. | terra: The denier does not urge feeding the needy, the precise social failure opposed by the pass's feeding scene.
terra: The worshippers يُرَآءُونَ, performing for others' gaze; this corrupt visible display sits beside their refusal of small aid in 107:7.
terra: The show-offs of 107:6 withhold even small aid, joining corrupted concern for human sight to failure of the mercy enacted by the pass.
